JUDGE PERMANENTLY TOSSES Trump Suit Against Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Letter
sources.text:
A federal judge in Miami has permanently dismissed President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on a birthday letter allegedly sent to Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin P. Gayles, an Obama appointee, issued an order on Saturday granting the Journal's motion to dismiss with prejudice, meaning the president cannot refile another lawsuit over the same issue. The ruling was first reported by the Washington Examiner.
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements" that caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.
The Letter at the Center of the Dispute
The Journal published a story on July 17, 2025, describing a sexually suggestive birthday note allegedly gifted to Epstein for his 50th birthday in 2003. The note includes typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what appears to be a woman, with Trump's signature at the bottom near the figure's pelvic region.
According to the Journal's reporting, the note ends with the line: "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret." The letters were reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence for her involvement in Epstein's sex-trafficking scheme.
Trump vehemently denied responsibility for the text, the signature and the artwork. A copy of the birthday letter was later released through the House Oversight Committee.
The Journal's article came as the second Trump administration faced intense scrutiny over whether it had withheld documents about Epstein's alleged sex crimes, despite promises of transparency.
Judge: President 'Grasping at Straws'
Gayles had previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.
In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 decision in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which requires public figures to prove that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth — the standard known as "actual malice."
"The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote, adding that the president was "grasping at straws" with the $10 billion case, according to NPR.
POLITICO reported that Gayles found Trump's attorneys had failed to credibly allege "actual malice" in the complaint against the paper.
Wider Legal Battles With the Press
The ruling is a setback for Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, the president is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.
Online, a post from an Instagram account summarized the development with a brief caption noting that a federal judge had dismissed the president's lawsuit, reflecting how quickly the story circulated among supporters and critics alike.
Our Take
The president deserves a legal system that treats him fairly, and this ruling shows us exactly what happens when the same old rules are applied by the same old players. A judge appointed by Barack Obama — a man whose administration weaponized federal agencies against its political enemies — has now permanently shut the door on Trump's effort to hold the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch accountable. And he did it with a smirk, calling the president's case "grasping at straws."
Folks, this is the game: the legacy media can publish whatever it wants, no matter how damaging or allegedly fabricated, and as long as they can hide behind the "actual malice" shield, there is no recourse. The 1964 Sullivan standard was designed for a different era — one before a handful of corporate press barons coordinated a daily assault on the legitimacy of a sitting president.
But here is the truth: Trump has spent years fighting these battles, and he has won far more than he has lost. The American people understand that the corporate press is not their friend — they are the mouthpiece of the very establishment that Trump was elected to dismantle. This ruling is a temporary setback, not a final verdict. The president will keep fighting, and he has the support of millions of patriots who see the media for what it is.
So we ask you, folks: should a sitting president have the right to hold the press accountable when it publishes false and defamatory claims? Or does the media's "actual malice" shield amount to a license to lie? Let us know what you think.

President Donald Trump’s $10 billion legal battle with The Wall Street Journal just hit a brick wall in a Miami courtroom.
And the judge didn’t exactly cushion the impact.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the president’s defamation lawsuit Saturday, accusing Trump’s attorneys of “grasping at straws” in their attempt to establish that the newspaper deliberately published false information about a purported birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein.
The ruling was issued with prejudice, which means Trump cannot simply submit another revised complaint and start over in the same case.
But there is one rather important detail in this legal drama.
The judge did not rule that Trump wrote the letter.
He ruled that Trump’s lawyers failed to meet the demanding legal standard required to sue a news organization for defaming a public figure.
Those are two very different questions, although you’d hardly know it from some of the coverage celebrating the dismissal.
The controversy began in July 2025, when The Wall Street Journal published an article describing a sexually suggestive birthday greeting allegedly bearing Trump’s name.
The letter was reportedly part of a collection assembled by Ghislaine Maxwell for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003.
According to the newspaper, the message included a drawing resembling a naked woman and ended with the words:
“Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret.”
Trump has repeatedly denied writing or signing the letter.
He called the newspaper’s reporting “false, malicious, and defamatory” and filed suit against the Journal, its parent companies, Rupert Murdoch and the reporters responsible for the story.
The original complaint sought at least $20 billion across two defamation counts. The amended case at issue Saturday sought $10 billion.
The stakes were considerable, even by Trump lawsuit standards.
And the dispute wasn’t merely between the president and an unfamiliar news organization.
Murdoch, whose media empire includes Fox News and the Journal, has long been a major figure in conservative media.
The lawsuit turned a bitter disagreement over Epstein reporting into a courtroom confrontation between two of the most recognizable names in American politics and media.
Gayles had already dismissed Trump’s original complaint in April, but he gave the president’s attorneys another opportunity to make their case.
They submitted an amended complaint in May.
On October 31, the judge concluded that the revised version still failed to establish actual malice.
That is the legal standard established by the Supreme Court’s 1964 decision in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan.
For public officials to prevail in this type of defamation case, they generally must establish that the publisher knew the disputed statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for its truth.
Gayles wrote: “The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice.”
He described the allegations as vague, conclusory and sometimes inconsistent with the Journal’s own article.
The judge also rejected the suggestion that the newspaper had concealed Trump’s denial.
As Gayles observed, the Journal had informed readers that Trump called the letter fake and denied writing it.
That mattered because Trump’s attorneys were trying to establish that the newspaper knowingly or recklessly published false information.
The judge concluded that their allegations did not plausibly support that claim.
There was another significant development after the Journal’s original reporting.
In September 2025, the House Oversight Committee obtained a redacted copy of Epstein’s birthday book from his estate.
The material included a page resembling the letter described by the newspaper.
That provided public evidence that such a page existed in the birthday collection.
It did not independently establish who created or signed it.
Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt rejected the suggestion that its appearance settled the controversy.
“It’s very clear President Trump did not draw this picture, and he did not sign it,” she said.
Trump has maintained that position throughout the dispute.
The document’s existence and its authorship are separate issues, and the court’s dismissal did not resolve the latter.

The statement continued:
“The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.”

Dow Jones, meanwhile, offered a much shorter reaction.
“We’re pleased with the court’s decision,” a spokesperson said.
The legal result is a significant victory for the newspaper, which successfully defended its reporting against Trump’s defamation claims.
It also illustrates just how difficult it is for a president, or any other prominent public figure, to prevail in a defamation lawsuit against a media organization.
The First Amendment provides substantial protection for reporting about public officials, even when the subjects insist that the reporting is wrong.
Trump’s lawyers will now have to decide how to challenge the dismissal on appeal.
And the controversy that produced the lawsuit remains unresolved in one important respect.
Trump says he never wrote the Epstein birthday letter.
The Journal stands by its reporting.
The judge has dismissed the defamation case.
But the question of who actually created the disputed birthday greeting wasn’t answered in Saturday’s ruling.
For all the courtroom fireworks, that distinction is still worth keeping in the headlines.

He also disagreed with Trump on how the article characterized his denial, writing that “it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.”

Trump’s lawyers argued that the outlet “falsely, maliciously, and defamatorily” accused Trump of writing the alleged birthday letter. They added in their motion to deny the defendants’ motion to dismiss the case that the outlet never “attempted to prove” that Trump wrote the letter in the article or in the legal case.
“Authorship is not merely something Defendants cannot prove — it is something they never even attempted to prove. They never identified the source of the letter, authenticated the signature, or explained how they attributed the typewritten text to President Trump,” Trump’s lawyers wrote in a filing.
The outlet reported that the alleged birthday letter, detailed in its story, was part of an album of letters from friends and acquaintances that Epstein’s accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, compiled for his 50th birthday. The outlet wrote that the letter and album came before Epstein was first arrested on sex crime charges.

Trump’s lawyers also took issue with the fact that the authors of the story “had no corroboration from Maxwell” in their story. Gayles called this argument a “red herring.”
Trump, who has stated that he cut off ties with Epstein years before Epstein’s initial arrest, was seeking no less than $10 billion in financial and reputational damages from the defendants.

sources.news_title: Judge Dismisses Trump’s Defamation Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal Publisher
sources.text:
A federal judge on Oct. 31 dismissed President Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal’s publisher and other defendants over an article about a birthday letter allegedly sent to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The dismissal was with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot file another amended complaint. Trump had sought $10 billion in the lawsuit.
In his ruling, Gayles wrote that Trump was “grasping at straws.”
The judge noted that Trump’s complaint said the defendants only “reviewed” the letter but did not have a copy of it in their possession.
“The Court cannot discern any substantive difference—and certainly not one that would establish actual malice—between Defendants reviewing the Letter before publication and obtaining a copy of the Letter. Defendants reviewed the Letter and later reported on its contents. Nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy,” Gayles wrote.
The July 2025 article by The Wall Street Journal described a letter bearing Trump’s name in an album assembled for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003. According to the article, the letter included typewritten text framed by a drawing of a naked woman.
Trump denied writing the letter, drawing the image, or signing it. The judge’s ruling stated that during an interview with the Department of Justice, Ghislaine Maxwell, an associate of Epstein’s, said, “subject to penalty of perjury for lying to a federal officer,” that she did not remember that Trump submitted a letter for Epstein’s 50th birthday.
Trump sued on July 18, 2025, and filed an amended complaint in May after the court dismissed his original complaint.
In August 2025, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform subpoenaed the Epstein estate for all letters in the birthday book. The Epstein estate complied and included a copy of the birthday book. The court also found a letter that matched the description in the Wall Street Journal article.
Gayles rejected Trump’s argument that publishing despite his denials demonstrated actual malice. The judge noted that The Wall Street Journal included Trump’s denials.
“In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a ‘fake,’ Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story. But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” Gayles wrote.
“The article details a thoughtful and detailed investigation,” he wrote.
The judge wrote that if that were the law, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation.
The Wall Street Journal also did not ignore Trump’s denial but allowed readers to make up their own minds.
The judge cited reporters’ efforts to contact Trump, his team, Justice Department officials, the FBI, Maxwell, and others involved with the birthday album.
The defendants include Dow Jones, News Corp., Rupert Murdoch, Robert Thomson and journalists Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo.
Gayles left unresolved whether defendants could recover attorneys’ fees under state laws protecting against lawsuits targeting public participation. He gave them 30 days to file a motion addressing which state’s law applies and whether they qualify for reimbursement of their legal expenses.
Citing an 11th Circuit ruling, Gayles said requiring publishers to defend groundless defamation lawsuits through costly discovery could discourage reporting on public figures and undermine First Amendment protections.
The White House referred an Epoch Times request for comment to Trump’s personal counsel.

sources.text:
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles has dismissed with prejudice the amended $10 billion defamation lawsuit that President Donald Trump brought against The Wall Street Journal. The ruling ends Trump’s second effort to challenge the paper’s reporting on a birthday card it said he sent to Jeffrey Epstein more than two decades ago, reports NBC News.
Gayles found that the revised complaint did not clear the high bar public figures must meet in defamation cases. Trump failed to plausibly show that the Journal published the story with actual malice.
The judge wrote, “As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed. And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate.”
Court examines claims about the 2003 birthday book and related statements
The Journal’s story, published last July, described a birthday book that Ghislaine Maxwell compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003. The book appeared to contain a card from Trump, who was friends with Epstein at the time. Trump filed the original suit shortly after the article appeared. He later refiled the $10 billion lawsuit after a judge threw out the first one.
The card featured a hand-drawn outline of a naked woman with what looked like Trump’s first name signed in the pubic area. It also held a typewritten note that presented an imaginary conversation with Epstein. Trump has denied any role in creating the card.
The lawsuit accused the paper of inventing the note and asserted that no such document existed. It alleged that the writers “falsely represent as fact that President Trump drew the naked woman’s breasts and signed his name ‘Donald’ below her waist, ‘mimicking pubic hair.’” The complaint further said the article caused Trump “overwhelming financial and reputational harm.”
Epstein’s estate later released a card that matched the Journal’s description. Trump and the White House have said the document is a fake. The suit also argued that the paper’s decision not to publish an image of the card in the original story showed that “no authentic letter or drawing exists.” The House Oversight Committee later released the card after obtaining it from the estate.
The complaint contended that the Journal should have known the story was false because Trump denied it. It noted that the paper did not interview Maxwell, who is serving 20 years in prison on sex trafficking charges. The original article stated that reporters wrote her a letter requesting an interview and included a comment from her attorney.
Attorneys for the Journal said the revised suit came “nowhere close” to proving actual malice. They described the required showing as one in which “the false statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.”
The lawyers stated that “the Article itself established that the Journal not only investigated” the matter but also “informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.” They added, “There is nothing inherently defamatory about sending a bawdy letter to a friend.”
They noted that the article “emphasizes that the Birthday Book was created before Epstein was first arrested” and “makes clear that President Trump’s friendship with Epstein ended years before Epstein was charged with sex crimes.” The attorneys also argued that the later public release of the card showed the story was “substantially true.”
Maxwell acknowledged assembling the birthday book during an interview last year with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche. She said she could not remember whether Trump contributed to it.
The White House has maintained that the signature does not belong to Trump and differs from his distinctive full signature. Democrats gathered documents in which Trump signed only his first name, and those signatures appear very similar to the one on the card.

On Saturday, Judge Darrin P. Gayles of U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted the Journal’s request that the complaint be dismissed, writing that the president “has failed” to prove that the Journal had “acted with actual malice.”
Actual malice is a legal standard that must be met by public figures in defamation proceedings. It means the defendants knew what they were publishing was false or acted with reckless disregard for the truth.

Judge Throws Out Trump's Epstein Lawsuit for Good After Saying He Was 'Grasping at Straws' Against WSJ
A Miami judge found Trump failed to show actual malice, though his legal team plans to appeal
A federal judge in Miami has permanently dismissed Donald Trump's £7.5 billion ($10 billion) defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal over its reporting on a birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein, ruling that the former president was 'grasping at straws' and had failed to show the paper acted with 'actual malice'.
US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles threw out the case with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled in the same court. Trump's camp says the fight is not over and plans to press on.
Second Bid Thrown Out 'With Prejudice'
Gayles dismissed the suit with prejudice on Saturday 31 October in a 20-page ruling, CBS News reported. The judge found that Trump had not shown the defendants published defamatory statements with actual malice, the legal standard a public figure must meet.
A dismissal with prejudice bars Trump from refiling the same claims in the same court. He can still appeal the ruling.
'As with his first attempt, he has failed,' Gayles wrote, MeidasNews reported. In April, the same judge dismissed the original complaint, finding that Trump came 'nowhere close' to showing actual malice. Trump's legal team then filed an amended version.
The judge said the amended suit was 'grasping at straws' in trying to 'manufacture' flaws in the newspaper's reporting, CBS News reported.
Disputed Birthday Letter at Centre of Case
The case grew out of a July 2025 Journal report on a sexually suggestive birthday letter bearing Trump's name. The letter appeared in a 2003 album that Ghislaine Maxwell assembled for Epstein's 50th birthday.
According to MeidasNews, the letter featured a drawing of a naked woman and a typewritten exchange between Trump and Epstein. Its closing line wished Epstein a happy birthday and added: 'may every day be another wonderful secret.'
The Journal's story ran as the Trump administration faced mounting pressure over its handling of the Epstein files. Trump called the story 'FAKE' and denied writing or signing the letter. He sued the Journal, its publisher Dow Jones, parent company News Corp, News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson, chairman emeritus Rupert Murdoch, and reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo, seeking £7.5 billion ($10 billion), NBC News reported.
House lawmakers later subpoenaed Epstein's estate and obtained a redacted copy of the birthday book, which included the letter. Karoline Leavitt, then White House press secretary, said at the time: 'It's very clear President Trump did not draw this picture, and he did not sign it.'
Judge Rejects Claims of 'Sloppy' Reporting
Trump's lawyers argued that the reporters saw the letter without obtaining a physical copy and failed to properly investigate Maxwell's role. Gayles rejected that argument.
According to the ruling, the Journal contacted Trump and his representatives, sought comment from the Justice Department and the FBI, tried to reach Maxwell and approached others connected to the album. The paper also included Trump's denials in its original coverage, MeidasNews reported. Gayles described the work as a 'thoughtful and detailed investigation.'
'In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a "fake," Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story,' the judge wrote.
Trump's team leaned on Maxwell's later interview with the Justice Department, in which she said she did not remember Trump submitting a birthday letter. That interview took place after the article was published. Gayles called the Maxwell references 'a red herring' and said they did not show the journalists knew they were publishing falsehoods.
The judge did not rule on the letter's authenticity or on the truth of the Journal's reporting. His decision addressed a narrower question: had Trump plausibly alleged that the paper knowingly published falsehoods or recklessly disregarded the truth? Twice now, Gayles has concluded that he had not.
Trump Signals Appeal as Fees Fight Looms
A spokesperson said Trump 'will continue to press forward' with the lawsuit against the Journal and the other defendants, CBS News reported. A source familiar with his legal strategy said the decision will likely be appealed.
The defendants are also seeking attorneys' fees and costs under anti-SLAPP laws, which are designed to deter lawsuits that target free speech. Gayles found Trump's claims lacked merit but did not award fees, because it remains unresolved which state's law, Florida's or New York's, governs the case, MeidasNews reported.
The defendants have 30 days to file a motion on that question. The judge has not awarded fees. If the defendants succeed, Trump could be ordered to cover the legal costs of the Journal and the other defendants.
The actual malice standard dates to the Supreme Court's 1964 ruling in New York Times Co v Sullivan. It requires public figures suing for defamation to show that a defendant published a defamatory falsehood knowing it was false or with reckless disregard for its truth, a deliberately high bar meant to protect robust reporting on powerful people.
For now, the ruling hands the Journal a clear win in a case that pitted a sitting president against one of the country's most prominent newspapers and the Murdoch media empire behind it.

A federal judge dismissed President Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, delivering the latest setback in his broader legal campaign against major U.S. news organizations.
In an order issued Saturday, U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Trump's suit against the newspaper, its parent companies and two reporters with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled in their current form.
The lawsuit stemmed from a July 2025 Journal article reporting on a purported birthday letter sent to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump denied authoring the letter and sued the newspaper, alleging defamation.
Read More on Politics
Gayles ruled that Trump failed, for a second time, to plausibly allege that the defendants acted with "actual malice," the constitutional standard public figures must meet to prevail in defamation cases. The judge repeatedly cited the landmark Supreme Court decision New York Times v. Sullivan, which established heightened protections for press coverage of public officials.
"The costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit ... could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether," Gayles wrote while explaining why public figures must plausibly allege actual malice at the outset of litigation.
The court also rejected Trump's argument that the Journal acted recklessly by publishing the article after he denied its central claim.
"In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a 'fake,' Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story," Gayles wrote. "But that is not what the actual malice standard requires."
The ruling marks one of the most significant court defeats yet for Trump's recent efforts to use defamation litigation against major media outlets.
Pending: Trump's $10B Lawsuit Against BBC
Trump is suing the BBC in a federal court in Miami regarding a Panorama documentary that spliced together portions of Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech. The suit seeks $5 billion in damages for each of the two counts listed—one count of defamation and one count of violating a Florida trade practices law.
While the BBC apologized for the edit, the outlet denies defamation.
"As we have made clear previously, we will be defending this case," a BBC spokesperson said in December 2025.
Trump has been ordered to sit for a deposition by December 11, and the judge warned Trump this week that the case could be dismissed if he does not produce more relevant documents or evidence showing his legal team's search for them.
Pending: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Lawsuit
Three media outlets filed a First Amendment lawsuit in September after Trump banned them from the White House and escorted reporters off the White Houst grounds.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico argued that the ban was retaliation for unfavorable coverage and violated the First Amendment and due-process protections.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump, granted a temporary restraining order on September 24 and ordered the White House to restore the outlets' credentials. He said they were likely to succeed on their claim that the administration revoked access without adequate standards or due process.
He converted the order to a preliminary injunction on October 14 to keep the outlets in the White House while the case proceeds. He found they were likely to prevail on both First Amendment and due-process claims. Kelly wrote that Trump's own statements suggested the ban was motivated by displeasure with the outlets' coverage, making it likely unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
The outlets amended their complaint on October 28 to argue that even though White House credentials were restored, the Trump administration was excluding them from pool assignments in the Oval Office and on Air Force One. They are asking the court to restore that access as well.
Pending: Trump's $15B Lawsuit Against the New York Times
Trump sought $15 billion in damages from The New York Times, several of its reporters and Penguin Random House over reporting and the book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father's Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success.
A federal judge dismissed the defamation lawsuit in September 2025.
U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday, appointed by Republican President George H.W. Bush, said Trump's filing violated rules requiring a clear and concise explanation for relief, adding that a lawsuit is not "a public forum for vituperation and invective" or "a protected platform to rage against an adversary."
"A complaint is not a megaphone for public relations or a podium for a passionate oration at a political rally or the functional equivalent of the Hyde Park Speakers' Corner," Merryday wrote.
Rather than ending the case, however, Merryday allowed Trump to file an amended complaint. Trump later submitted a revised version, and the litigation remains pending.
Pending: Trump's Lawsuit Against Pulitzer Board
Trump is suing members of the Pulitzer Prize Board over a 2022 statement defending the Pulitzer Prizes awarded to The New York Times and The Washington Post for reporting on Russian interference in the 2016 election.
Trump argues the statement was defamatory. The case has survived dismissal efforts and remains active in Florida, where discovery and pretrial proceedings are continuing.
In December 2025, the Pulitzer Prize Board asked a Florida court to compel Trump to hand over his tax returns, financial records, and full medical and psychological files in a sweeping discovery request aimed at testing his claims of reputational and emotional harm.
A spokesperson for the Pulitzer Board told Newsweek: “Just like any other plaintiff, the president must articulate and prove his claims with evidence."
In August, the judge in the case was removed after the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a complaint alleging that the judge who ruled that Trump's case could proceed was being considered for a federal appointment.

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, sought $10 billion in damages.

In a deal announced on December 14, 2024, ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward Trump's presidential library and issue a public apology to settle a defamation lawsuit over inaccurate statements made by anchor George Stephanopoulos during a broadcast earlier this year.
The lawsuit was filed after Stephanopoulos said during a March 10 segment of ABC News' This Week while interviewing Representative Nancy Mace, a South Carolina Republican, that Trump had been "found liable for rape."

In his lawsuit, Trump had accused Stephanopoulos of acting with "actual malice."

Trump sued The Des Moines Register, Gannett and veteran pollster J. Ann Selzer over a final 2024 Iowa poll that showed then-Vice President Harris leading in the state before Trump ultimately won it.
The lawsuit sought substantial damages and alleged the poll was deceptive and amounted to election interference. An Iowa judge dismissed the case in September, finding the poll and related reporting were protected speech.

A US federal judge on Saturday dismissed US President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), its parent company and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a report detailing his alleged links to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
US District Judge Darrin Gayles, ruling in Miami, dismissed the case with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot file the same lawsuit again. The judge said the President had failed to establish that the defendants published defamatory statements with actual malice, a legal requirement for public figures pursuing defamation claims.
"Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote in his ruling, adding that the newspaper had carried out a "thoughtful and detailed investigation" before publishing the report, according to Reuters.
The dismissal is a setback for Trump, who has repeatedly clashed with media organisations over coverage critical of him. The President has frequently accused news outlets of spreading "fake news" and has pursued several legal battles against media organisations during his second term.
WHAT WAS THE WALL STREET JOURNAL REPORT ABOUT?
The lawsuit stemmed from a WSJ report published last year about a sexually suggestive letter and drawing allegedly bearing Trump's name in a birthday album prepared for Epstein's 50th birthday in 2003.
The album was reportedly compiled by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell, who was associated with Epstein. The letter, according to the newspaper, contained text surrounded by the outline of what appeared to be a hand-drawn naked woman.
It ended with the words, "Happy Birthday -- and may every day be another wonderful secret."

Sullivan, which established that public figures must demonstrate that a publication knowingly carried false information or acted with reckless disregard for the truth to win a defamation case.

A federal judge in Florida has tossed a revised version of President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit against The Wall Street Journal over a story about a birthday card he allegedly sent Jeffrey Epstein more than two decades ago.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles found Trump’s amended suit suffered from the same fatal flaw as his first attempt — it fell far short of the high legal bar to show the paper had published the story with “actual malice.”
“As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed. And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate,” the judge wrote.
Trump first sued the paper last July, shortly after the Journal published a story about a birthday book that Ghislaine Maxwell had assembled for Epstein’s 50th birthday in 2003. The book appeared to include a card from Trump, who had been friends with Epstein around that time.
The card contained a hand-drawn outline of a naked woman with what appeared to be Trump’s first name signed in the pubic area. It included a typewritten note depicting an imaginary conversation with Epstein, who would later be charged with sex trafficking.
Trump denied having anything to do with the card, and his suit accused the paper of having made it up and that no such note existed.
Epstein’s estate later released a copy of a card matching the Journal’s description. Trump and the White House maintain the document is a fake.
Trump’s suit alleged the writers of the article “falsely represent as fact that President Trump drew the naked woman’s breasts and signed his name ‘Donald’ below her waist, ‘mimicking pubic hair,’” and that the article caused him “overwhelming financial and reputational harm.”
Trump’s suit also criticized the paper for not publishing an image of the card in the initial story, saying that shows “no authentic letter or drawing exists” — even though the House Oversight Committee publicly released the card after getting it from the Epstein estate.
The suit says the Journal should have known the story was bogus because Trump said it was not true. It also chided the paper for failing to interview Epstein co-conspirator Maxwell, who’s serving 20 years in prison on sex trafficking charges. The story said Journal reporters wrote her a letter asking for an interview and included a comment from her attorney.
The paper’s attorneys argued that like the original suit, Trump’s revised suit came “nowhere close” to demonstrating the paper acted with actual malice, in which “the false statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.”
Despite Trump’s claim the paper failed to properly investigate the card before publishing the story, “the Article itself established that the Journal not only investigated” but also “informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it,” the paper said in its motion to dismiss the suit.
Further, the attorneys argued, alleging that someone sent another person a birthday card is not defamatory.
“There is nothing inherently defamatory about sending a bawdy letter to a friend,” the attorneys wrote, and the article “emphasizes that the Birthday Book was created before Epstein was first arrested” and “makes clear that President Trump’s friendship with Epstein ended years before Epstein was charged with sex crimes.”
The attorneys also contended the suit should be dismissed because the public release of the card shows the story was “substantially true.”
In an interview last year with then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Maxwell acknowledged assembling the birthday book but said she could not remember whether Trump contributed to it.
The White House maintains the signature is not Trump’s and that it looks different from his distinctive full signature. Democrats compiled a number of documents where Trump signed just his first name over the year, and the signatures appear very similar to the one on the card.

For the second time this year, US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles ruled that Trump failed to plausibly allege that the Rupert Murdoch-owned newspaper acted with “actual malice” when it published the story.
Gayles rejected the president’s argument that The Journal should have withheld its story after he denied writing the letter, saying such a requirement would violate the First Amendment.

The ruling is another stinging defeat in the president’s legal crusade against the American news media and is sure to be celebrated by the press freedom groups that have denounced Trump’s suits.
Gayles previously dismissed the $20 billion lawsuit in April, ruling that Trump’s original complaint relied on “formulaic” assertions of malice that came “nowhere close” to the legal standard for a public figure.

The case was especially unusual because Trump brought it while serving as president. Legal analysts who spoke with CNN said they could not recall another instance of a sitting president suing a news outlet over a story.
However, it was also part of a recognizable, long-running pattern for Trump — using the courts to pressure news organizations over unflattering coverage of him.
During his second term, Trump has also filed a $15 billion defamation case against The New York Times over its coverage of his 2024 campaign. President Trump contends that these statements are false because he (1) did not author, sign, or draw any portion of the Letter or direct anyone else to author it; (2) never made or dictated to anyone any of the statements in the voiceover or had any such conversation with Epstein as portrayed in the Letter; and (3) was not "childhood pals" with Epstein….
The court concluded that Trump hadn't actually alleged "actual malice," which is to say knowing or reckless falsehood:

[b.] Denial is not Enough
Though vague, the Amended Complaint appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice. Moreover, the Article did not ignore or minimize President Trump's denial. Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it. President Trump and his team responded with his denial, the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment. Defendants also attempted to speak with Maxwell; she did not respond to their request and her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court. In addition, Defendants reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book, who confirmed that Weitz put the book together. Connaughton (1989), supports his position that Defendants' purported failure to investigate is enough to support an inference of actual malice. However, in Harte-Hanks, the Supreme Court expressly stated that "[a]lthough failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category. Here, President Trump has not alleged any facts, beyond conclusory allegations, that support an inference that Defendants purposefully avoided the truth.}
Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation. First, it alleges that the investigation was lacking because Defendants only reviewed the Letter but did not have a copy in their possession. The Court cannot discern any substantive difference—and certainly not one that would establish actual malice—between Defendants reviewing the Letter before publication and obtaining a copy of the Letter. Defendants reviewed the Letter and later reported on its contents. Nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy.
In addition, President Trump's focus on Maxwell is entirely misplaced. The Eleventh Circuit has found "allegations that the Defendants failed to fully investigate their statements by intentionally choosing not to speak with any witnesses who could have refuted the allegedly defamatory statements" insufficient to plead actual malice. And any argument that Defendants "purposely avoided" the truth by either not disclosing what Maxwell told them or by refusing to speak with her is difficult to reconcile with President Trump's own allegations.
The Amended Complaint alleges that "Maxwell has stated, subject to penalty of perjury for lying to a federal officer, that she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th birthday." Based on this allegation, Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation. In short, references to Maxwell are a red herring and simply do not establish that Defendants "actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account[] or was highly aware that the account was probably false."
[d.] Omissions
President Trump's argument that the Article omits certain facts does not save his claims. First, how or why the voiceover in the Letter was typewritten or how the voiceover was confirmed to be in the third person are inconsequential details that have no bearing on whether Defendants published the Article knowing its contents were false or with reckless disregard as to its falsity. Moreover, Defendants' decisions about how to investigate and what to include in the Article do not establish malice. "Obviously the author of an article will have to choose which facts to include and which to omit. It is impossible to print all of the facts on which an opinion or belief is based …. Were the courts or criticized [parties] to be allowed to dictate the contents of such articles, censorship would have won out over free speech and the right to dissent."
Finally, the allegation that Defendants intentionally omitted President Trump's denial that he signed the Letter or a discussion on whether the signature on the Letter is authentic, is belied by the Article. It states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that "[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared." . This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he "signed" the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic.
[e.] The September 8 Article
The Amended Complaint's reliance on the September 8 Article to establish malice is equally unavailing. Nothing in the law suggests that a journalist must report on every piece of evidence they uncover before going to print. Moreover, it is unclear why President Trump argues the September 8 Article shows that his signature "could not be more different" than the one in the Letter, when it contains several examples where President Trump's actual signature and sketches are similar to those in the Letter. At bottom, the September 8 Article does not support a finding that Defendants knew or should have known that President Trump did not sign the Letter….

sources.news_title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
sources.text:
'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
A federal judge has dismissed President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein
Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal’s investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.
Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists.
The White House did not immediately react publicly to Saturday's dismissal or respond to an AP request for comment.
The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.
The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.
The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story “false, malicious, and defamatory.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements,” which, it alleged, caused “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president.
Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.
In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.
“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.”
The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, “Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.”
Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

sources.news_title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
sources.text:
A federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejudice President Donald Trump's amended defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter from the president to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
District Court Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump had again failed to plausibly allege the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025.
"As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which came more than six months after he dismissed Trump's first version of the suit. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."
By dismissing the suit with prejudice, the judge blocked Trump from filing another suit alleging the same claims about Murdoch and the paper in federal court.
Gayles said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation," and he rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.
The judge did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter. Trump has adamantly denied writing it.
When Galyes first dismissed the suit in April, he allowed Trump to file an amended version of the complaint to cure legal defects the judge had identified.
Trump was seeking $10 billion in damages from Murdoch and the Journal, which is owned by Murdoch's News Corp.
A spokesperson for the newspaper's publisher, Dow Jones & Co., in a statement to CNBC on Saturday, said, "We're pleased with the court's decision."
A spokesman for Trump's legal team confirmed to CNBC that the president plans to appeal the ruling.
"President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," the spokesman said in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."
Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending the letter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."
Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to Supreme Court decisions that Gayles cited at the beginning of his ruling.
Trump's amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told the president "I will handle it" during a phone conversation they had about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature, Newsweek previously reported.
Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and that the article was published after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.
Gayles said that accepting that last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.
Saturday's ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media.
Another federal judge in Miami on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The Journal's article on July 17, 2025, said a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday.
The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.
The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker."
"A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article.
"The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.
Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'
"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

A US judge dismissed Mr Trump’s case against the Wall Street Journal and media magnate Rupert Murdoch, which had targeted a report alleging the president sent Epstein a birthday letter.
Mr Trump sought $10 billion in damages after the Wall Street Journal published a July 2025 story describing what it said was a 2003 letter to Epstein that apparently included a drawing of a naked woman.
Mr Murdoch is the founder of News Corp. which owns the Wall Street Journal.
The Journal’s report intensified pressure on Mr Trump not only from Democrats but also from within his own Republican party, where lawmakers dismissed his efforts to characterize the matter as a hoax and demanded the full release of legal records connected to Epstein.
In his decision, Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed Mr Trump’s lawsuit with prejudice, preventing him from filing a revised complaint — a step Mr Trump previously took after Judge Gayles rejected an earlier version of the case in April.
Judge Gayles wrote that, in both attempts, Mr Trump did not meet the standard required for his defamation claim, failing to show the defendants “acted with actual malice”.
The note consists of a short dialogue between ‘Donald’ and ‘Jeffrey’
The House Oversight Committee last year released a copy of what it described as Mr Trump’s birthday note to Epstein, presenting it as a brief dialogue between “Donald” and “Jeffrey”.
“We have certain things in common,” says Donald, to which Jeffrey responds: “Yes, we do, come to think of it.”
“Enigmas never age, have you noticed that?” asks Donald.
“As a matter of fact, it was clear to me the last time I saw you,” says Jeffrey.
“A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday – and may every day be another wonderful secret,” the note ends, followed by Mr Trump’s signature.
Epstein files
The report piled scrutiny on Mr Trump from both Democrats and his own Republican party
For years, many of Mr Trump’s supporters have fixated on the Epstein case, embracing the belief that “deep state” elites were shielding a network of Epstein associates — particularly among Democrats and in Hollywood.
Mr Trump spent months battling to block the Department of Justice from publishing the so-called “Epstein Files”, but he ultimately signed legislation passed by Congress that required the documents to be made public.
His name appears repeatedly in the released materials, though he denies wrongdoing and has not been charged with any criminal offenses related to the matter.
Other prominent figures have seen their reputations collapse over links to Epstein, including Britain’s former prince Andrew.
With the 3 November US midterm elections looming — contests set to determine which party controls Congress — Democrats have reportedly poured more than $35 million into advertising tied to Epstein.
Since taking office in January 2025, Mr Trump has faced relatively limited political resistance due to Republican control of both the House and Senate, a dynamic that has placed added weight on the courts as a check on his agenda.
In another legal dispute yesterday, plaintiffs filed a new lawsuit seeking to block Mr Trump’s effort to build a massive triumphal arch in front of the iconic military cemetery outside Washington.
The arch is part of a broader set of initiatives Mr Trump has promoted to leave a personal imprint on the capital, alongside plans for a White House ballroom and an extensive renovation of the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.
On Friday, a US federal judge questioned government claims that the proposed arch — which Mr Trump has said would contain drones and snipers — was justified on national security grounds.
“It’s something (the) region needs militarily and I think aesthetically also,” Mr Trump told reporters late last night.
“We’re going to see if we can get it built.”

WASHINGTON: Seorang hakim persekutuan di Florida semalam bertindak membatalkan saman fitnah bernilai AS$10 bilion (RM44 bilion) yang dikemukakan oleh Presiden Amerika Syarikat (AS) Donald Trump terhadap akhbar The Wall Street Journal.
Hakim Daerah AS, Darrin Gayles memutuskan bahawa saman terpinda yang dikemukakan oleh Trump mengalami kelemahan undang-undang yang sama seperti percubaan pertamanya berikutan kegagalan membuktikan unsur ‘niat jahat sebenar’.

Memuatkan artikel berkaitan…
Hakim berkenaan turut menegaskan bahawa pembatalan saman itu dilakukan dengan prejudis, sekali gus menghalang pihak Trump daripada mendaftarkan semula kes berkenaan di mahkamah pada masa hadapan.
Saman berkenaan pertama kali dikemukakan oleh Trump pada Julai lalu selepas akhbar itu menerbitkan laporan berhubung sebuah buku hari lahir yang dikumpul oleh Ghislaine Maxwell untuk ulang tahun ke-50 pesalah seks, Jeffrey Epstein pada tahun 2003.
Buku berkenaan mengandungi sekeping kad yang memaparkan lakaran wanita tanpa pakaian beserta tanda tangan nama pertama Trump pada bahagian sensitif lakaran itu, selain nota bertaip yang mengandungi perbualan rekaan bersama Epstein.

Pihak Trump dan Rumah Putih kekal dengan pendirian bahawa dokumen berkenaan adalah palsu dan mendakwa laporan akhbar itu telah merosakkan reputasi serta memberi impak kewangan yang serius kepada beliau.
Trump turut mengkritik akhbar berkenaan kerana tidak menemubual Maxwell yang kini menjalani hukuman penjara 20 tahun atas pertuduhan pemerdagangan seks, walaupun wartawan terbabit telah menghantar surat permohonan temu bual dan memasukkan kenyataan peguamnya. – AGENSI

The album was compiled by Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein's associate. Trump denied writing the letter and accused the newspaper of fabricating the report to damage his reputation.
The court rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should have abandoned the story following his denial, emphasising the First Amendment protections afforded to journalists.
An earlier version of the $10 billion lawsuit was dismissed in April 2026, but Trump was allowed to amend and refile his complaint.

Judge rules on Trump’s $10 billion WSJ-Epstein lawsuit
A federal judge has permanently dismissed US President Donald Trump’s $10 billion amended defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a report about his letter to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
In July 2025, the WSJ published an article describing a sexually suggestive note, which Trump allegedly presented to the disgraced financier for his 50th birthday in 2003. It reportedly appeared in a book of congratulatory letters put together by Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for her participation in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.
The note, which, among other things, said: “Happy Birthday – and may every day be another wonderful secret,” contained several lines of typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what looks to be a nude woman. A signature resembling the one used by Trump appeared in the area where the figure’s pelvic region might be.
Following the publication, the US president vigorously denied the authorship of the raunchy birthday card, claiming: “This is not me. This is a fake thing. I never wrote a picture in my life. I don’t draw pictures of women.”
Trump’s initial defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and Murdoch’s News Corp., which owns the outlet, was rejected by US District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami in April. However, he allowed the president’s team to fix the legal defects that he had identified and file another complaint.
On Saturday, the same judge threw out Trump’s second attempt to sue the WSJ and Murdoch, saying that “as with his first attempt, he has failed” to prove that the defendants acted with actual malice when they reported on the birthday card.
Gayles disagreed with Trump’s lawyers, who argued that the outlet should have dropped the story as soon as the president denied his involvement with Epstein. “That is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” he wrote in a 20-page ruling.
The judge dismissed the case “with prejudice,” meaning that it cannot be refiled again.
A spokesperson for the WSJ’s publisher, Dow Jones & Co., said in a statement that it’s “pleased with the court’s decision.”
The representative of Trump’s legal team insisted that “the president will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.” A source told CBS News that the ruling by Gayles will likely be appealed.
Trump has repeatedly denied having been friendly with Epstein, who died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. However, the US president’s name is mentioned on at least 3,000 occasions in a massive trove of files related to the investigation of Epstein’s case, which had been released by the US Department of Justice last year.

Trump Loses Defamation Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal
A US federal judge has dismissed Donald Trump's defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal, preventing him from filing the case again.
The ruling, delivered by Federal Judge Darrin P. Gayles, marks the second time the lawsuit has been rejected. Although the court dismissed the initial case in April, Trump was allowed to submit an amended complaint in an attempt to strengthen his claims.
However, Gayles concluded in a new 20-page ruling that Trump had failed to establish “actual malice”, a key legal requirement in his defamation claim. In an earlier decision, the judge said the president had come “nowhere close” to proving defamation.
Trump originally filed the lawsuit in July last year at a federal court in Miami, Florida. He named several individuals and organisations as defendants, including the Wall Street Journal’s publisher, Dow Jones, its parent company News Corp, media owner Rupert Murdoch, News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson, and journalists Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo.
The legal action followed a controversial report published by the newspaper concerning a birthday album reportedly prepared for the late financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003.
According to the report, Trump allegedly contributed a letter to the album for Epstein’s 50th birthday. The publication claimed that the message contained a sexually suggestive drawing of a naked woman alongside a handwritten-style signature bearing Trump’s name.
The newspaper described the contents of the alleged letter as follows:
“The letter bearing Trump’s name, which was reviewed by the Journal, is bawdy—like others in the album. It contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker. A pair of small arcs denotes the woman’s breasts, and the future president’s signature is a squiggly “Donald” below her waist, mimicking pubic hair.
Also included with the picture was an imaginary conversation between Trump and Epstein.”
Trump strongly rejected the allegations, insisting that he neither produced the drawing nor wrote the birthday message.
When the report first appeared, he described the alleged birthday contribution as “fake” and attacked the publication, calling it a “disgusting and filthy rag.”
The controversy also brought renewed attention to Trump’s past association with Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire financier who died in 2019 while facing sex trafficking charges. His death was officially ruled a suicide.
Epstein’s former girlfriend and longtime associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, is serving a 20-year prison sentence following her conviction for sex trafficking. The US Department of Justice said she worked with Epstein in carrying out the crimes.
The case has also featured prominently in political discussions surrounding the release of government records relating to Epstein.
Trump faced criticism from some of his prominent supporters after dismissing claims that Epstein had trafficked girls for influential associates as a “hoax”.
When the Justice Department released documents connected to the investigation, many contained redactions. The department maintained that Epstein had trafficked girls for his own purposes rather than for high-profile associates.
The latest court decision closes Trump’s current defamation case against the newspaper, following two dismissals. The ruling centres on his failure to establish the legal requirements for his claim and does not, by itself, determine whether the newspaper’s underlying report was factually accurate.
